settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The utility is a test/build-support class in an Arquillian adapter module; its primary use appears to be unpacking locally downloaded TomEE distributions rather than processing remote user uploads.

No validation, containment check, or canonicalization exists in the method, but no caller reachable with untrusted data was confirmed inside the read span, so no end-to-end attack path is demonstrated.
When noparent is true (line 52-54) only the leading directory component is removed by the regex; this does not mitigate embedded '../' segments and is not a guard against traversal.
candidates.description: In arquillian-tomee-common's Zips.unzip(File, File, boolean) (lines 34-78) each archive entry name is taken verbatim (line 51: String path = entry.getName();), optionally with only the first path segment stripped when noparent is true (line 53), and then combined with the caller-supplied destination via new File(destination, path) (line 55). The parent directory is created (line 62) and the entry content is streamed to that file (line 63). There is no normalization (e.g. File.getCanonicalPath) and no check that the resolved path is still contained within the destination directory, so an entry name containing '../' segments (or an absolute path on platforms where new File(parent, child) honors it) causes content to be written outside the intended extraction root. This is a candidate for a Zip Slip / archive path traversal weakness in a utility used for unpacking downloaded distributions and libraries. It is reported as a candidate only: the read span does not establish which callers supply archives influenced by an attacker, and the security impact depends entirely on the trust level of the archive and destination.
missing_evidence: The source of the File arguments for each Zips.unzip call site (e.g. Setup.downloadFile output, maven-plugin distribution extraction) and whether any such archive can be supplied or modified by an attacker.
Whether an archive containing '../' entries is realistic in the deployment contexts where this class is used.
Files.assertDir / Files.writable / Files.mkdir implementations (not read) to see whether any downstream path validation occurs.
Behavior on Windows versus POSIX for new File(parent, child) with backslash/absolute entry names.
preconditions: An archive processed by Zips.unzip contains an entry whose name includes path-traversal sequences (e.g. '../') or an absolute path.
Some reachable caller passes an archive whose contents are attacker-influenced (or untrusted by design) to Zips.unzip, which was not established from the read source.
The JVM process has write permission to the directory that the traversal resolves to.
candidates.title: Zip Slip: Zips.unzip joins raw ZIP entry names onto the destination directory without containment check
